question: A team is building a customer support agent that lets Claude call a search_tickets tool. They want to block adversarial users from convincing the assistant to ignore its support-only scope and instead answer unrelated requests. Before the main conversation turn is sent to Claude, they want a cheap, fast check that flags obviously abusive input. What should they implement?
options: A) A instruction embedded inside the search_tickets tool_result content telling Claude to refuse off-topic requests, since tool_result content carries the same authority as the system prompt
B) A lightweight model call that classifies the incoming user message with a constrained structured output before it reaches the main conversation, so abusive input is filtered pre-emptively
C) A second full-size Claude call that repeats the entire conversation history at maximum thinking effort, since more reasoning always produces a more reliable safety classification
D) A regular expression list of banned words applied to the final assistant response only, since screening after generation catches every abusive pattern the input might have contained
correct_answers: B) A lightweight model call that classifies the incoming user message with a constrained structured output before it reaches the main conversation, so abusive input is filtered pre-emptively
explanations: Incorrect. Content inside tool_result blocks is treated by Claude as untrusted data, not as instructions with system-prompt authority, so placing guidance there is unreliable for enforcing scope.

Correct. A harmlessness screen using a lightweight model (e.g. Claude Haiku) with structured output to classify input before it reaches the main conversation is the documented pattern for cheap, fast pre-screening of user input.

Incorrect. Repeating the full conversation at maximum thinking effort is expensive and is not how lightweight input screening is designed; the documented approach uses a smaller, faster model for this check.
Incorrect. Regex word lists on the output alone don't catch adversarial framing in the input and are easily bypassed by rephrasing; they are not the documented pre-screening mechanism.
